Debt Sustainability


Debt sustainability analysis – for example, as practiced currently by the International Monetary Fund – substantially improves the ability to predict future sovereign debt crises.



Details on IMF debt sustainability analysis are here: https://www.imf.org/en/About/Factsheets/Sheets/2023/imf-world-bank-debt-sustainability-framework-for-low-income-countries

column5: Debt sustainability is a complex issue and depends on political as well as economic factors. The IMF methodology is not perfect but it's better than nothing.
column8: The fiscal rules that have been used in the past, don't take into account interest rates and other important factors that are included in the debt sustainability analysis.
column11: Difficult to know how the independent fiscal councils would operate in practice.  In particular, they may not be that independent.

column5: Not an exact science but still helps.
column8: Existing rules are unworkable, with many problems. No silver bullet but a good reform, although the technicalities still need some work.

column5: it gives a clear sense of trajectories and uncertainty under existing policies.
column8: too many factors have to take into account to be able to write down a simple and good rule.

column5: The issue is, of course, the politics. It is very hard for a multilateral institution, not just the Fund, to make an objective SSA given the stakes for the country. A recent case in point is Argentina.
column8: Given the political economy considerations plaguing a multilateral institution worried about impacting future market access for the country in question , the more flexible and open to interpretation and assumptions the analysis, the less credible. Rules need predictability.

column5: It's not really intended to predict sovereign crises but to help steer policy away from high risk zones.  Current IMF DSA is better in this respect than what came before.
column8: It's a bit better than what is there now, but still too much fixation on 3% and 60% and on expenditure as the control variable.
column11: A retreat to national level assessment would be a move in the wrong direction.

column5: Debt sustainability analysis helps issuers to increase their debt level because IMF serves as a neutral agent assessing their repayment capacity. However, repayment capacity is only a necessary condition for redemption, as willingness to repay is also needed.
column8: I disagree because sustainability assessment will only increase debt levels without forcing countries to restructure their debt if levels have risen by too much... For the latter, a European sovereign debt restructuring scheme would be needed - but it is still lacking...
column11: I would definitely prefer councils over rules, but I would also prefer the twin set of no debt limits coupled with a credible restructuring regime over both options mentioned in the question.

column5: The purpose of DSA is not to predict debt crises but to propose a sustainable path with implications for requirements of external support or debt restructuring, easing of terms (maturities, interest rates).
column8: This is a misguided use of DSA. See comment on previous question.

column5: In absolute terms, prediction performance is poor. But relative to other approaches, DSA fares well.
column11: It depends on the institutional support.

column8: Existing existing EU fiscal rules are dormant. Switching to debt sustainability rules would be economically and politically sound. A fresh start with a better framework
column11: Fiscal policy is inherently a political issue. Fiscal councils serve best as non-partisan fact providers. "Independent" fiscal councils are mirage because a democracy cannot commit to future fiscal policy. They become irrelevant once they go against current government

column5: High levels of debt especially when short maturity and in foreign currency can indicate a future debt crisis.
column8: Current approach has many pitfalls: no separate treatment of investments, no consideration of assets or of type of debt, etc.
column11: Although an interesting idea in principle, fiscal councils have not worked out that well (e.g. Swedish experience).

column5: Debt crises are very often reflecting multiple equilibria. DSA ignores that, unless assumed by the author. That's not forecasting, it's making assumptions.
column8: The proposal would be a serious improvement, in spite of adopting DSA! The progress is to move to the long run.
